newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW-Trenwick seeks to boost value.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Trenwick seeks to boost value.

text.p: Trenwick Group Inc is considering a number of options to boost shareholder value, including share buybacks and acquisitions, the company's chief financial officer said.
The Stamford, Conn.-based reinsurer also would consider a sale of the company but is not actively seeking a buyer, Alan Hunte told Reuters in a telephone interview on Thursday.
"We're always looking for transactions and if somebody wants to pay up for the company, then we're prepared to consider that too," he said.
But, he said, "I wouldn't describe us as actively looking to sell the company.
"We don't have a 'for sale' sign on the company," he added. "But are we prepared to sell the company? Absolutely -- at the right price."
Hunte's comments come after Lehman analyst Peter Wade last week initiated coverage of Trenwick with an outperform rating.
Wade, in his research report, cited expectations for share buybacks and deal activity, including a possible sale of the company.
Trenwick, like other reinsurers, is considering its strategic alternatives as intense competition and declining prices put pressure on growth.
Just last week Bermuda excess liability insurer EXEL Ltd agreed to acquire the shares of property catastrophe reinsurer GCR Holdings Ltd it did not already own for $637 million.
And last summer, General Re Corp agreed to buy National Re and Germany's Muenchener Rueckversicherungs-Gesellschaft (Munich Re) agreed to buy American Re.

"There's many companies who are doing virtually the same thing we are, looking for either merger partners or an acquisition or something to be able to grow the business because that's really the only way you're going to really do it with the market today," Hunte said.
Hunte said the company has been looking for acquisitions for several years and said it would prefer to stick with what it knows as a broker market reinsurer.
But, he said, "The landscape is pretty sparse in terms of companies that you'd either want to acquire or merge with."
In addition, he noted that acquisitions of broker market reinsurers can be virtually impossible if the deal is not friendly because the business is based almost entirely on relationships.
However, he said, there might be some opportunities outside the United States.
As for a possible sale of the company, Hunte said declined to comment on speculation that the company might be willing to accept an offer of $41 a share, or about 1.5 times book value.
But any deal would have to be done at a premium, he said.
And, "I'm just not sure that people are prepared to pay the kind of premium we might be looking for," he said.
Trenwick was unchanged at 32-5/8 on Friday afternoon, giving it a market value of about $360 million.
Meanwhile, he said, share buybacks are always an option for Trenwick and noted that the company has a history of repurchasing stock.
"If we think it's opportunistic to do that, we will do it," he said.
However, he said the company does not currently have board authorization to buyback stock.
Lehman's Wade has said he expects share repurchases to be substantial over the next two years, reducing Trenwick's share count by 16 percent and six percent in 1997 and 1998 respectively.
